items.topic: inference-t2 · inference-t3 · complete sufficient statistic and UMVU estimation
items.stem: For n≥2, let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from the density f(x|θ)=θx^(θ−1), 0<x<1, where θ>0 is unknown. Which estimator is the uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator of 1/θ?
items.explanation: Put Yᵢ=−ln Xᵢ. For 0<Xᵢ<1, Yᵢ is positive. Its distribution is exponential with rate θ, so E(Yᵢ)=1/θ. Therefore E[(1/n)∑Yᵢ]=1/θ: the sample mean of the Yᵢ values is unbiased for the quantity asked. Since Y=∑Yᵢ has a Gamma distribution with shape n and rate θ, it is a complete sufficient statistic for θ. The estimator Y/n is a function of this complete sufficient statistic and is unbiased; by the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem it is UMVU. Replacing Yᵢ by −ln Xᵢ gives −(1/n)∑ln Xᵢ, option A. Other-exam relevance: this exponential-family, transformation and UMVU reasoning is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Source-key audit: the supplied answer-key page lists all four options for Q1, but the question asks for one UMVU estimator. Direct calculation gives E[−(1/n)Σln Xᵢ]=1/θ, and the statistic is a function of the complete sufficient Gamma sum, so option A alone is UMVU. The other listed expressions do not have expectation 1/θ. The bank records the mathematically derived answer and flags the printed key discrepancy.

items.topic: inference-t1 · minimal sufficiency for a normal model with parameter-dependent mean
items.stem: For n≥2, let ε₁,…,εₙ be independent N(0,σ²) random variables and suppose Yᵢ=iα+i²α²+εᵢ, i=1,…,n, where α∈ℝ and σ>0 are unknown. Which of the following is a jointly minimal sufficient statistic for (α,σ²)?
items.explanation: The observations are independent normal variables with common variance σ² and means μᵢ=iα+i²α². The joint density is proportional to exp{−[1/(2σ²)]∑(Yᵢ−iα−i²α²)²}. Expand the square: ∑Yᵢ²−2α∑iYᵢ−2α²∑i²Yᵢ+∑(iα+i²α²)². The last term depends only on the known indices and α. Thus all sample dependence in the likelihood is through the three quantities ∑Yᵢ², ∑iYᵢ and ∑i²Yᵢ, making option A sufficient by factorisation. For this full two-parameter normal family, the likelihood-ratio criterion also shows that equality of the likelihood ratio for all (α,σ²) requires these three summaries to agree; hence the statistic is minimal sufficient. The other options omit at least one likelihood-dependent summary or use a different, insufficient quantity. Other-exam relevance: the same factorisation and minimal-sufficiency ideas are useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where statistical inference is in the syllabus. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations. Source-status note: the supplied answer-key page marks Q2 as “Dropped”. items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · inference-t3 · shifted exponential: sufficiency, completeness and UMVU
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample with density f(x|θ)=e^(θ−x) for x≥θ and 0 otherwise, where θ is unknown. Let X̄ be the sample mean and X₍₁₎=min(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which of the following combinations of statements is correct?
statements: X̄ is the method-of-moments estimator of θ.
X₍₁₎ is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ.
X₍₁₎−1/n is the uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator of θ.
X₍₁₎ is a sufficient statistic for θ.

A.why: E(X)=θ+1, so equating X̄ to the population mean gives θ̂MM=X̄−1, not X̄.

B.why: The likelihood increases with θ over the allowed range θ≤X₍₁₎, so its maximum occurs at X₍₁₎.

C.why: The minimum has an exponential excess with mean 1/n. Subtracting 1/n removes its bias; completeness and sufficiency give the UMVU result.

D.why: The joint density depends on the observations through their minimum and a factor independent of θ. The factorisation theorem therefore gives sufficiency.

items.explanation: Step 1: The support condition requires θ≤X₍₁₎. The likelihood is L(θ)=exp(nθ−ΣXᵢ) for θ≤X₍₁₎ and zero otherwise. Since exp(nθ−ΣXᵢ) increases as θ increases, the largest allowed value, X₍₁₎, is the MLE. Step 2: E(X)=θ+1, so the method-of-moments estimate solves X̄=θ+1 and is X̄−1. Step 3: X₍₁₎ has mean θ+1/n, so X₍₁₎−1/n is unbiased. The minimum is also complete and sufficient in this shifted-exponential model, so the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem identifies it as UMVU. Thus statements 2, 3 and 4 are true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · constrained MLE for a normal mean
items.stem: A random sample is 3, 6, 9 from a normal distribution with unknown mean μ restricted to μ≤5 and known variance 1. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of μ?
items.explanation: For a normal distribution with known variance, the likelihood is largest at the sample mean when μ is unrestricted. Here X̄=(3+6+9)/3=6. But μ is not allowed to exceed 5. We therefore maximise the likelihood over μ≤5. The allowed value closest to the unrestricted maximum 6 is the boundary μ=5. Hence the constrained MLE is 5 (option B). The key lesson is to check the parameter space before reporting the sample mean. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · sufficiency and completeness
items.stem: Which combination of statements about sufficient statistics, complete statistics and maximum-likelihood estimators is correct?
statements: A maximum-likelihood estimator need not be unique.
Every complete statistic is automatically sufficient.
A sufficient statistic need not be complete.
Every function of a sufficient statistic is sufficient.

A.why: Likelihoods can have more than one maximiser, so an MLE need not be unique.

B.why: Completeness is a property of expectations of functions of a statistic. It does not by itself imply sufficiency.

C.why: Sufficiency means no additional sample information about the parameter is left after conditioning on the statistic. Completeness is a separate property.

D.why: A function of a sufficient statistic can discard information. Only one-to-one transformations are guaranteed to preserve sufficiency.

items.explanation: The correct statements are 1 and 3. Sufficiency and completeness answer different questions. A sufficient statistic retains all sample information about the unknown parameter. A complete statistic has no non-zero function whose expectation is zero for every parameter value. One property does not automatically imply the other. Also, a many-to-one function of a sufficient statistic may lose information; for example, replacing a sample sum by its square can merge distinct values. Finally, a likelihood can be flat over an interval, giving several maximisers. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t5 · method of moments
items.stem: A discrete random variable has P(X=1)=2(1−θ)/(2−θ) and P(X=2)=θ/(2−θ), where 0<θ<1. If X̄ is the sample mean, what is the method-of-moments estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The method of moments equates a sample moment to the corresponding population moment. Here the first population moment is E(X)=1·P(X=1)+2·P(X=2). Substitute the probabilities: E(X)=2(1−θ)/(2−θ)+2θ/(2−θ)=2/(2−θ). Set X̄=2/(2−θ). Multiply by (2−θ): X̄(2−θ)=2. Thus 2X̄−X̄θ=2, so X̄θ=2X̄−2 and θ̂MM=2(X̄−1)/X̄=2(1−1/X̄). Option C. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations. items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE with parameter-dependent support and non-unique maximisers
items.stem: The observations 0.80, 0.71, 0.90, 1.20, 1.68, 1.40, 0.88 and 1.62 come from a Uniform(θ−0.2, θ+0.8) distribution. Which listed value is a maximum-likelihood estimate of θ?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 48 (December 2018) on page 23. The supplied answer list on page 63 ends at Question 44, so no printed answer-key entry for Q48 is available; the result is derived directly. For every observation to lie inside the Uniform(θ−0.2, θ+0.8) interval, the lower endpoint must be below the sample minimum and the upper endpoint above the sample maximum. The minimum is 0.71, so θ−0.2<0.71 gives θ<0.91. The maximum is 1.68, so 1.68<θ+0.8 gives θ>0.88. Therefore every θ in the feasible interval (0.88,0.91) gives the same likelihood, because the density height is 1/(0.8+0.2)=1. The MLE is not unique. Of the listed choices, 0.9 lies in that interval, so option B is an MLE. Other-exam relevance: maximum likelihood, uniform location families, parameter-dependent support and non-unique maximisers are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · inference-t4 · sufficiency, completeness, bias and consistency
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(0,3θ), θ>0, and define Tₙ=(1/3)max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which statement is NOT true?
options: Tₙ is a sufficient statistic for θ
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 54 (December 2017) on page 28. The supplied answer list on page 63 ends at Question 44, so no printed key is available; the result follows from the distribution of the sample maximum. Let Mₙ=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). For 0<m<3θ, P(Mₙ≤m)=[m/(3θ)]ⁿ, so the density of Mₙ is n m^(n−1)/(3θ)ⁿ. Its expectation is E(Mₙ)=3θ·n/(n+1), giving E(Tₙ)=θ·n/(n+1), which is not θ. Thus Tₙ is biased, and statement B is the one that is NOT true. Since n/(n+1)→1 and Mₙ/(3θ)→1 in probability, Tₙ is consistent. The likelihood depends on the sample only through Mₙ, so Mₙ (and hence Tₙ) is sufficient. The sample maximum in a Uniform(0,3θ) scale family is also complete: if Eθ[g(Mₙ)]=0 for every θ>0, then the integral of g(m)m^(n−1) over (0,3θ) is zero for every upper limit, forcing g=0 almost everywhere. Therefore A, C and D are true. Option B is the only statement that is not true. Other-exam relevance: order statistics, sufficiency, completeness, unbiasedness and consistency are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · MLE for a uniform scale parameter
items.stem: A random sample X₁,…,Xₙ is drawn from Uniform(0,5θ), where θ>0. Let X₍ₙ₎=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). What is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The joint density is (1/(5θ))ⁿ when all observations are between 0 and 5θ, and zero otherwise. The support condition requires 5θ≥X₍ₙ₎, or θ≥X₍ₙ₎/5. Within this allowed region the likelihood (1/(5θ))ⁿ decreases as θ increases. To maximise it, choose the smallest allowed θ. Therefore θ̂MLE=X₍ₙ₎/5, option D. items.topic: inference-t4 · constrained normal MLE, bias, sufficiency and consistency
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. N(μ,1), where μ∈[0,∞). Let μ̂ be the maximum-likelihood estimator of μ. Which statements are true?
items.explanation: The likelihood for μ is proportional to exp{−(1/2)Σ(Xᵢ−μ)²}, with μ restricted to be nonnegative. Without the restriction, the likelihood is maximised at the sample mean X̄ₙ. If X̄ₙ≥0, this value is allowed; if X̄ₙ<0, the largest likelihood over μ≥0 occurs at the boundary μ=0. Therefore μ̂=max(X̄ₙ,0), so statement 1 is true. For statement 2, take μ=0: X̄ₙ is symmetric about zero, and max(X̄ₙ,0) is positive on half the outcomes and zero otherwise, so its expectation is positive rather than zero. Thus μ̂ is not unbiased. The normal likelihood factorises through X̄ₙ, so statement 3 is true. Finally X̄ₙ→μ in probability and the maximum function is continuous; for μ≥0 its transformed limit is μ. Thus μ̂ is consistent and statement 4 is true. The printed answer key identifies statements A, C and D. Other-exam relevance: constrained maximum likelihood, sufficiency, bias and consistency are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those other examinations.
statements: μ̂=max(X̄ₙ,0).
μ̂ is unbiased for μ.
X̄ₙ is sufficient for μ.
μ̂ is a consistent estimator of μ.

A.why: The unconstrained normal likelihood is maximised at X̄ₙ. Restricting μ to [0,∞) projects this value onto the allowed parameter space, giving max(X̄ₙ,0).

B.why: At μ=0, μ̂=max(X̄ₙ,0) is positive with positive probability and has positive expectation, so it is not unbiased for every μ≥0.

C.why: For a normal sample with known variance, the joint density factors through X̄ₙ. Restricting the parameter space does not remove this sufficiency.

D.why: X̄ₙ converges in probability to μ. The function x↦max(x,0) is continuous and equals μ at every μ≥0, so μ̂ is consistent.

items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t4 · sufficient statistic and MLE for a Pareto-type model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. with density f(x|θ)=θ/x² for x≥θ and 0 otherwise, where θ>0. Define X₍₁₎=min(X₁,…,Xₙ) and X₍ₙ₎=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which statements are correct?
items.explanation: Write the joint likelihood: L(θ)=θⁿ/(X₁²⋯Xₙ²) when 0<θ≤X₍₁₎, and L(θ)=0 otherwise. For sufficiency, separate it as gθ(X₍₁₎)h(X₁,…,Xₙ): the factor involving θ and the support restriction depends on the sample through X₍₁₎, while h=1/(∏Xᵢ²) is free of θ. Thus X₍₁₎ is sufficient. The product-based quantity in statement 2 alone is not sufficient because it does not determine X₍₁₎ and hence cannot determine the support restriction. For the MLE, within the allowed range 0<θ≤X₍₁₎, θⁿ increases as θ increases. The largest allowed value is therefore θ̂MLE=X₍₁₎. X₍ₙ₎ is not the MLE. So statements 1 and 4 only are correct. Other-exam relevance: sufficient statistics, factorisation and maximum-likelihood estimation are useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where inference is in the syllabus. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.
statements: X₍₁₎ is a sufficient statistic for θ.
1/(n∏ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ²) is a sufficient statistic for θ.
X₍ₙ₎ is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ.
X₍₁₎ is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ.

A.why: The joint density is [θⁿ/(∏Xᵢ²)] I(0<θ≤X₍₁₎). The sample enters the parameter-dependent support through X₍₁₎, so the factorisation theorem gives sufficiency.

B.why: This quantity does not retain the sample minimum. Two samples can have the same product but different minima, and therefore different likelihood support in θ; it is not sufficient.

C.why: The likelihood is zero when θ exceeds the sample minimum. The maximum observation does not determine the largest allowed θ.

D.why: On 0<θ≤X₍₁₎, the likelihood is proportional to θⁿ and increases with θ. Its maximum is attained at θ=X₍₁₎.

items.topic: probability-t1 · inference-t4 · order statistics, bias and consistency
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(0,θ+1), where θ is unknown and θ+1>0. Let Tₙ=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which combination of statements is correct?
statements: Tₙ is a consistent estimator of θ.
Tₙ is an unbiased estimator of θ.
Tₙ−1 is a consistent estimator of θ.
limₙ→∞ Eθ(Tₙ)=θ+1.

A.why: Tₙ approaches the upper endpoint θ+1, not θ.

B.why: Its expectation is n(θ+1)/(n+1), which is not θ.

C.why: The sample maximum approaches the upper endpoint θ+1, so subtracting 1 makes it approach θ.

D.why: The expectation n(θ+1)/(n+1) tends to θ+1.

items.explanation: For a Uniform(0,b) sample, the expected maximum is nb/(n+1). Here b=θ+1, so E(Tₙ)=n(θ+1)/(n+1). As n increases, this expectation tends to θ+1, not θ; hence Tₙ is not a consistent estimator of θ. The maximum itself approaches θ+1, so Tₙ−1 approaches θ and is consistent. The expectation limit in statement 4 is also correct. Thus statements 3 and 4 are true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: probability-t1 · inference-t4 · order statistics, bias and consistency
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from Uniform(θ,θ+1), where θ is unknown. Let Tₙ=min(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which combination of statements is correct?
statements: Tₙ is an unbiased estimator of θ.
limₙ→∞ Eθ(Tₙ)=θ.
Tₙ is a consistent estimator of θ.
max(X₁,…,Xₙ) is a consistent estimator of θ.

A.why: The minimum has expectation θ+1/(n+1), so it is biased upward for finite n.

B.why: θ+1/(n+1) tends to θ as n grows.

C.why: The sample minimum approaches the lower endpoint θ, so it is consistent.

D.why: The sample maximum approaches the upper endpoint θ+1, not θ.

items.explanation: For a Uniform(θ,θ+1) sample, the expected minimum is θ+1/(n+1). This is not exactly θ for finite n, so the minimum is biased upward. However, the extra term 1/(n+1) tends to zero. Therefore E(Tₙ) tends to θ, and the sample minimum itself converges to θ. The sample maximum converges to θ+1, so it does not estimate θ consistently. Statements 2 and 3 are true. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. items.topic: inference-t4 · non-unique MLE for a uniform location family
items.stem: A sample of size 11 from Uniform(θ−1,θ+1) is: −0.71, 0.30, −0.40, −0.63, −0.81, −0.70, 0.10, −0.01, 0.02, −0.96, −0.92. Which listed values are maximum-likelihood estimates of θ?

A.why: The feasible interval is −0.70<θ<0.04, so −0.96 is outside it.

B.why: The value 0.30 is also outside the feasible interval.

C.why: 0.02 lies strictly between −0.70 and 0.04, so it is an MLE.

D.why: −0.54 lies strictly between −0.70 and 0.04, so it is also an MLE.

items.explanation: For Uniform(θ−1,θ+1), every observation must lie inside the interval. The smallest observation is −0.96 and the largest is 0.30. The lower-end condition θ−1<−0.96 gives θ<0.04. The upper-end condition 0.30<θ+1 gives θ>−0.70. Therefore every θ in (−0.70,0.04) gives the same maximum likelihood. Among the four listed values, 0.02 and −0.54 lie in this interval. Both are MLEs; the estimate is not unique. Other-exam relevance: the same concept is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation or regression is in the syllabus. This is a syllabus-overlap note, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · consistency of estimators and convergence in probability
items.stem: Let X₁,…,X₂ₙ be independent and identically distributed N(μ,1) random variables, and let W be an independent standard Cauchy random variable. Which of the following statistics are consistent estimators of μ?
statements: T₁ₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ
T₂ₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁²ⁿXᵢ
T₃ₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿX₂ᵢ₋₁
T₄ₙ=(1/n)(∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ+W)

A.why: T₁ₙ is the average of n independent observations with mean μ. By the weak law of large numbers, T₁ₙ converges in probability to μ.

B.why: T₂ₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁²ⁿXᵢ=2[(1/(2n))∑ᵢ₌₁²ⁿXᵢ]. The bracketed average converges to μ, so T₂ₙ converges to 2μ, not μ in general.

C.why: The observations X₁,X₃,…,X₂ₙ₋₁ are still n independent and identically distributed N(μ,1) variables. Their average therefore converges in probability to μ.

D.why: T₄ₙ=X̄ₙ+W/n. Since W is a finite real-valued random variable, W/n converges to zero in probability. Slutsky's theorem then gives T₄ₙ converges in probability to μ.

items.explanation: Check each statistic separately. (1) The average of the first n independent N(μ,1) observations has mean μ and variance 1/n, which tends to zero. Hence it converges in probability to μ. (2) This statistic sums 2n observations but divides only by n. Its expectation is 2μ, not μ, so it is not generally consistent for μ. (3) The odd-indexed observations X₁,X₃,…,X₂ₙ₋₁ are still n independent observations from the same N(μ,1) distribution. Their average therefore has mean μ and variance 1/n, so it is consistent. (4) Rewrite T₄ₙ as the average of X₁,…,Xₙ plus W/n. A Cauchy variable does not have a finite mean or variance, but W/n nevertheless converges to zero in probability: P(|W/n|>ε)=P(|W|>nε) tends to zero for every ε>0. Thus adding W/n to a consistent average preserves its probability limit μ. The correct combination is 1, 3 and 4 only. Other-exam relevance: consistency and convergence-in-probability reasoning is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood when mean and variance share a parameter
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from N(θ,θ), where the normal distribution has mean θ and variance θ, with θ>0 unknown. What is the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ?
options: The maximum-likelihood estimator does not exist
items.explanation: For one observation, the normal density is proportional to θ^(−1/2) exp{−(x−θ)²/(2θ)}. For n independent observations, the log-likelihood, after dropping constants that do not depend on θ, is ℓ(θ)=−(n/2)logθ−[1/(2θ)]∑(Xᵢ−θ)². Expand the square: ∑(Xᵢ−θ)²=∑Xᵢ²−2θ∑Xᵢ+nθ². Differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to θ and set it equal to zero. This gives −n/(2θ)+(∑Xᵢ²)/(2θ²)−n/2=0. Multiply by 2θ²: −nθ+∑Xᵢ²−nθ²=0, or nθ²+nθ−∑Xᵢ²=0. Divide by n and solve the quadratic: θ=[−1±√(1+(4/n)∑Xᵢ²)]/2. Since θ must be positive and the square root is greater than 1 except in the degenerate all-zero case, the admissible root is the positive root with + before the square root. It is option B. The log-likelihood tends to −∞ as θ approaches zero and as θ tends to infinity, so this stationary point is the global maximum. Other-exam relevance: likelihood differentiation with a parameter shared by the mean and variance is useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where MLEs and normal models are in the syllabus. items.topic: inference-t7 · Bayesian estimation under squared-error and absolute-error loss
items.stem: Suppose X₁,…,Xₙ are independent observations from a normal distribution with unknown mean θ and known variance σ². The prior distribution of θ is normal with mean μ₀ and variance τ². Which statements about the Bayes estimators are correct?
statements: Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the mean of the posterior distribution.
Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the median of the posterior distribution.
Under absolute-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the median of the posterior distribution.
Under absolute-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the mean of the posterior distribution.

A.why: Under squared-error loss, the posterior mean minimises posterior expected squared loss.

B.why: The posterior is normal, so it is symmetric and its mean equals its median. Thus the posterior median is also the posterior mean in this question.

C.why: Under absolute-error loss, any posterior median minimises posterior expected absolute loss.

D.why: A normal posterior is symmetric, so its mean and median coincide. The posterior mean is therefore also a median in this question.

items.explanation: Bayesian estimation chooses the value that minimises the posterior expected loss. Under squared-error loss, the minimiser is the posterior mean. Under absolute-error loss, the minimiser is a posterior median. In this question the likelihood is normal and the prior is normal, so the posterior distribution is also normal. A normal distribution is symmetric, and its mean and median are the same. Therefore both the posterior mean and posterior median are the same number. That makes statements 1 and 2 true for squared-error loss, and statements 3 and 4 true for absolute-error loss. All four statements are correct. For completeness, the posterior variance is V=(n/σ²+1/τ²)⁻¹ and the posterior mean is V[(nX̄/σ²)+(μ₀/τ²)]. Other-exam relevance: conjugate Bayesian estimation and the link between loss functions and posterior summaries are useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where Bayesian estimation is in the syllabus. items.topic: inference-t4 · sampling distribution and bias of the normal MLE of variance
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent and identically distributed normal random variables with mean μ and variance σ². Let (μ̂,σ̂²) be the maximum-likelihood estimator of (μ,σ²). Which statements are correct?
statements: nσ̂²/σ² has a chi-square distribution with n−1 degrees of freedom.
σ̂² is an unbiased estimator of σ².
The variance of σ̂² tends to zero as n tends to infinity.
[n²σ̂⁴]/[(n−1)(n+1)] is an unbiased estimator of σ⁴.

A.why: The normal-sample result is ∑(Xᵢ−X̄)²/σ² ~ χ²(n−1). Since σ̂²=(1/n)∑(Xᵢ−X̄)², the correct scaling is nσ̂²/σ².

B.why: The MLE divides the residual sum of squares by n, so E(σ̂²)=(n−1)σ²/n, not σ².

C.why: Var(σ̂²)=2σ⁴(n−1)/n², which tends to zero as n tends to infinity.

D.why: If Q=nσ̂²/σ² ~ χ²(n−1), then E(Q²)=(n−1)(n+1). Hence E(σ̂⁴)=σ⁴(n−1)(n+1)/n², and the stated multiplier makes it unbiased for σ⁴.

items.explanation: For a normal sample, the maximum-likelihood estimator of variance is σ̂²=(1/n)∑(Xᵢ−X̄)². The standard normal-sample result is ∑(Xᵢ−X̄)²/σ² ~ χ²(n−1). Multiplying the MLE by n therefore gives nσ̂²/σ² ~ χ²(n−1), so statement 1 is true. Since a chi-square variable with n−1 degrees of freedom has mean n−1, E(σ̂²)=σ²(n−1)/n. This is not σ², so the MLE is biased downward and statement 2 is false. The same result gives Var(σ̂²)=2σ⁴(n−1)/n², which tends to zero, so statement 3 is true. To check statement 4, write σ̂⁴=(σ̂²)². If Q~χ²(n−1), then σ̂²=σ²Q/n and E(Q²)=(n−1)(n+1). Thus E(σ̂⁴)=σ⁴(n−1)(n+1)/n². Multiplying by n²/[(n−1)(n+1)] gives an unbiased estimator of σ⁴. Therefore statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct. Other-exam relevance: normal-theory sampling distributions, MLE bias and variance corrections are useful for UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics where estimation theory is in the syllabus. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · sufficient statistics for an exponential model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from an exponential distribution with unknown mean θ>0. Which of the following is NOT a sufficient statistic for θ?
items.explanation: For an exponential distribution with mean θ, the density of one observation is f(x|θ)=(1/θ)e^(−x/θ), for x>0. For an independent sample, the joint density is (1/θ)ⁿ exp{−(X₁+⋯+Xₙ)/θ}, provided all observations are positive. The sample enters the likelihood through the total S=X₁+⋯+Xₙ. By the factorisation theorem, S is sufficient for θ. Any one-to-one function of a sufficient statistic is also sufficient, so 1/S is sufficient. The pair (Xₙ, X₁+⋯+Xₙ₋₁) determines S by addition, so it also retains the sufficient statistic and is sufficient. But the ratio Xₙ/(X₁+⋯+Xₙ₋₁) does not determine S and does not retain all the information about θ in the likelihood. Hence option C is not sufficient. Other-exam relevance: the factorisation theorem and sufficiency for exponential families are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t2 · inference-t3 · inference-t4 · complete sufficient statistic and UMVU estimation in a normal model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent and identically distributed N(θ,σ²) random variables, where σ² is known. Write X̄=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ. Which expression is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of e^(2θ)?
items.explanation: Because the observations are normal with known variance, X̄ is sufficient for θ. It is also complete for this one-parameter normal location family. The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem says that an unbiased function of X̄ is the UMVU estimator. We use the moment-generating function of a normal random variable: if Z~N(μ,v), then E(e^(tZ))=exp(tμ+t²v/2). Here X̄~N(θ,σ²/n). Therefore E[e^(2X̄)]=exp(2θ+(2²/2)(σ²/n))=exp(2θ+2σ²/n). To remove the extra factor exp(2σ²/n), multiply by exp(−2σ²/n). Thus E[exp(2X̄−2σ²/n)]=e^(2θ), so option C is unbiased. Since it is a function of the complete sufficient statistic X̄, it is the UMVU estimator. Other-exam relevance: normal moment-generating functions, complete sufficiency and UMVU estimation are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.

items.topic: inference-t7 · Beta-Binomial conjugacy and Bayes estimation under squared-error loss
items.stem: In a clinical trial, let θ be the probability of recovery. A Beta(0.5,0.5) prior is assigned to θ. If 6 of 10 patients recover, which expressions are Bayes estimates of θ under squared-error loss?
items.explanation: For a binomial sample with 6 recoveries and 4 non-recoveries, the likelihood is proportional to θ⁶(1−θ)⁴. The prior Beta(0.5,0.5) has density proportional to θ^(−1/2)(1−θ)^(−1/2). Multiplying prior and likelihood gives a posterior proportional to θ^(6+0.5−1)(1−θ)^(4+0.5−1), so θ|data follows Beta(6.5,4.5). Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean: 6.5/(6.5+4.5)=6.5/11=13/22. Therefore option 1 is the numerical value and option 4 is the same posterior expectation written symbolically. Both are correct. Option 2 (11/20) is the observed sample proportion and is not the posterior mean here; option 3 is not the posterior mean either. Other-exam relevance: conjugate Bayesian estimation and posterior expected loss are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi; This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.
statements: E(θ | 6 of the 10 patients recovered)

A.why: The posterior is Beta(6.5,4.5), whose mean is 13/22. Option 4 is the same posterior expectation written symbolically, so statements 1 and 4 are true.

B.why: 11/20 is not the posterior mean for Beta(6.5,4.5).

C.why: 1/2 is not the posterior mean for Beta(6.5,4.5).

D.why: Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean E(θ|data). This is exactly the expression in statement 4 and equals 13/22 in statement 1.

items.topic: inference-t4 · bias of the constrained normal maximum-likelihood estimator
items.stem: Suppose X₁,…,Xₙ are i.i.d. N(θ,1), where θ≥0, and let T=max(X̄,0) be the maximum-likelihood estimator of θ. Which statement about its bias is correct?
options: There is θ₀>0 such that the bias is negative for 0<θ<θ₀ and positive for θ≥θ₀
items.explanation: The sample mean X̄ has distribution N(θ,1/n). The constrained MLE is T=max(X̄,0). For every realised value, max(X̄,0)≥X̄. Taking expectations gives Eθ(T)≥Eθ(X̄)=θ. Hence the bias Eθ(T)−θ is nonnegative for every θ≥0. At θ=0 the inequality is strict because a normal random variable has positive probability of being negative, and replacing its negative values by zero raises its expectation. For θ>0 the same truncation also makes the expectation larger than θ. Thus statement 1 is correct. Other-exam relevance: constrained MLEs and their finite-sample bias are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi; This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: inference-t7 · normal-normal conjugacy and Bayes estimation under squared-error loss
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. N(θ,1) random variables. Suppose the prior distribution of θ is N(0,σ²), where σ²>0. Under squared-error loss, let X̄=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ. What is the Bayes estimator of θ?
items.explanation: The sample likelihood, viewed as a function of θ, is proportional to exp{−n(θ−X̄)²/2}. It is a normal kernel with precision n. The prior N(0,σ²) has precision 1/σ². Combining the two normal kernels gives a posterior normal distribution with precision n+1/σ² and mean [nX̄]/[n+1/σ²]. Multiplying the numerator and denominator by σ² gives nσ²X̄/(1+nσ²). Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean. Therefore option 3 is correct. Other-exam relevance: normal conjugate priors and Bayes estimation are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · factorisation theorem for a uniform distribution on parameter-dependent triangular support
items.stem: Suppose (X₁,Y₁),…,(Xₙ,Yₙ) are independent observations from a distribution that is uniform on the triangle with vertices (0,0), (θ,0) and (0,θ), where θ>0. Which statistic is sufficient for θ?
items.explanation: The triangle is described by x≥0, y≥0 and x+y≤θ. Its area is θ²/2, so the uniform density is 2/θ² inside the triangle and zero outside. For n independent observations, the joint density is (2/θ²)ⁿ times an indicator that every observed point satisfies Xᵢ+Yᵢ≤θ. These inequalities are equivalent to maxᵢ(Xᵢ+Yᵢ)≤θ. The likelihood therefore depends on the sample through maxᵢ(Xᵢ+Yᵢ), and the factorisation theorem shows that this statistic is sufficient. Option 2 is correct. Other-exam relevance: sufficiency and parameter-dependent support are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · inference-t3 · Poisson complete sufficiency and UMVU estimation
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent and identically distributed Poisson(λ) random variables, where λ>0 is unknown. Which of the following statements about estimating e^(−2λ) are true?
statements: (1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ(−1)^(Xᵢ) is an unbiased estimator of e^(−2λ).
(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ(−1)^(Xᵢ) is a consistent estimator of e^(−2λ).
((n−2)/n)^(∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ) is the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of e^(−2λ).
((n−2)/n)^(∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ) is a consistent estimator of e^(−2λ).

A.why: The Poisson probability-generating function gives E[t^X]=exp{λ(t−1)}. At t=−1 this is e^(−2λ), so the sample average is unbiased.

B.why: The summands are i.i.d. and bounded between −1 and 1. The law of large numbers therefore gives convergence in probability of their average to e^(−2λ).

C.why: S=∑Xᵢ is complete and sufficient for λ. Conditional on S, X₁ has a Binomial(S,1/n) distribution, so E[(−1)^(X₁)|S]=(1−2/n)^S=((n−2)/n)^S. This conditional expectation is unbiased and is a function of the complete sufficient statistic, so Lehmann–Scheffé makes it the UMVU estimator.

D.why: S/n converges in probability to λ and n log(1−2/n) tends to −2. Hence (1−2/n)^S converges in probability to e^(−2λ).

items.explanation: Let S=∑Xᵢ. First use the Poisson generating function: E[t^X]=exp{λ(t−1)}. Substituting t=−1 gives E[(−1)^X]=e^(−2λ), proving statement 1. The variables (−1)^(Xᵢ) are independent, identically distributed and bounded, so their average converges in probability to its expectation by the law of large numbers; statement 2 is true. The sum S is sufficient and complete for λ in the Poisson family. Given S, the count X₁ is Binomial(S,1/n). Thus E[(−1)^(X₁)|S]=(1−2/n)^S. Rao–Blackwell and Lehmann–Scheffé show this is the UMVU estimator, proving statement 3. Finally, S/n→λ and n log(1−2/n)→−2, which gives (1−2/n)^S→e^(−2λ) in probability. Statement 4 is also true. All four statements are correct. Other-exam relevance: Poisson estimation, complete sufficiency, Rao–Blackwellisation and Lehmann–Scheffé are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · sufficient statistics for the variance of a zero-mean normal distribution
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. N(0,σ²) random variables, where σ²>0 is unknown. Which of the following statistics are sufficient for σ²?
statements: T₁(X₁,…,Xₙ)=(X₁,X₂,…,Xₙ).
T₂(X₁,…,Xₙ)=(X₁²,X₂²,…,Xₙ²).
T₃(X₁,…,Xₙ)=∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ².
T₄(X₁,…,Xₙ)=(X₁²+X₂², X₃²+X₄²+⋯+Xₙ²).

A.why: The full sample is sufficient because it retains every observation, so it cannot discard information about σ².

B.why: The vector of squares determines the sum of squares ∑Xᵢ², which is sufficient for σ².

C.why: The joint density is (2πσ²)^(−n/2) exp{−∑Xᵢ²/(2σ²)}. It depends on the sample through the sum of squares, so factorisation proves sufficiency.

D.why: Adding the two components of T₄ recovers ∑Xᵢ². Since T₄ determines a sufficient statistic, T₄ is also sufficient.

items.explanation: The joint density is (2πσ²)^(−n/2) exp{−(1/(2σ²))∑Xᵢ²}. By the factorisation theorem, S=∑Xᵢ² is sufficient for σ². T₁ is the complete observed sample, so it is sufficient. T₂ gives every squared observation and therefore determines S. T₃ is S itself. T₄ divides the squared observations into two groups, but adding its two components also gives S. Each statistic therefore determines a sufficient statistic, so all four are sufficient. The correct answer is option 4. Other-exam relevance: normal-family sufficiency and the factorisation theorem are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: inference-t2 · inference-t3 · identifying sample means that are UMVU estimators
items.stem: Consider a population with probability density or mass function fθ(x), depending on an unknown parameter θ. For an i.i.d. random sample X₁,…,Xₙ, let X̄ be the sample mean. In which of the following cases is X̄ the minimum-variance unbiased estimator of θ?
statements: fθ(x) is proportional to exp(−θx), for x≥0 and θ>0.
fθ(x) is proportional to exp(−(θ−x)²), for −∞<x<∞ and −∞<θ<∞.
fθ(x) is proportional to θˣ/x!, for x=0,1,2,… and θ>0.
fθ(x) is proportional to θˣ, for x=0,1,2,… and 0<θ<1.

A.why: This is an exponential distribution with rate θ, whose mean is 1/θ. The sample mean estimates 1/θ, not θ.

B.why: After normalisation this is a normal location family with mean θ and known variance 1/2. The sample mean is unbiased and is a function of the complete sufficient statistic ∑Xᵢ, so it is UMVU.

C.why: After normalisation this is a Poisson(θ) family. The sample mean is unbiased for θ and is the UMVU estimator because the sample sum is complete sufficient.

D.why: The normalised mass function is (1−θ)θˣ, a geometric distribution on {0,1,…} with mean θ/(1−θ), not θ.

items.explanation: Check each model separately. In case 1, the normalised density is θe^(−θx), whose mean is 1/θ, so X̄ does not estimate θ unbiasedly. In case 2, the density is a normal location model with mean θ and known variance 1/2. Its sample mean is unbiased, and the sample sum is complete sufficient; Lehmann–Scheffé therefore gives the UMVU result. In case 3, the model is Poisson(θ), so E(X̄)=θ. The sample sum is complete sufficient, making X̄ UMVU. In case 4, normalisation gives P(X=x)=(1−θ)θˣ, whose mean is θ/(1−θ), so X̄ is not unbiased for θ. Thus only cases 2 and 3 qualify. Other-exam relevance: UMVU estimation, exponential families and complete sufficient statistics are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · inference-t4 · complete sufficiency, ancillary statistics and covariance
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be a random sample from a normal distribution with unknown mean μ and known variance 1. Let X̄ be the sample mean and X₍₁₎=min{X₁,…,Xₙ}. Which statements are true?
statements: X̄ is a complete sufficient statistic for μ.
X̄ is a minimal sufficient statistic for μ.
X̄−X₍₁₎ is an ancillary statistic.
Cov(X̄,X₍₁₎)=0.

A.why: The normal location family with known variance is a full one-parameter exponential family. X̄ (equivalently the sum) is complete, sufficient and minimal sufficient.

B.why: The likelihood depends on μ through ∑Xᵢ, and the normal location family gives this statistic as minimal sufficient.

C.why: Adding a constant to every observation changes both X̄ and X₍₁₎ by the same amount. Their difference is unchanged, so its distribution does not depend on μ.

D.why: The covariance is positive, not zero. For a normal sample with unit variance, Cov(X̄,X₍₁₎)=1/n by the normal location identity for the sample minimum.

items.explanation: For a normal sample with known variance 1, the likelihood depends on μ through ∑Xᵢ, or equivalently X̄. This is a full one-parameter exponential family, so X̄ is complete and sufficient; the likelihood-ratio criterion also gives minimal sufficiency. For statement 3, shift every observation by μ: both the sample mean and sample minimum shift by μ, so their difference does not change. Its distribution is therefore free of μ, which is the definition of an ancillary statistic. Statement 4 is false. A useful identity for a standard normal sample is Cov(∑Xᵢ, X₍₁₎)=1; dividing by n gives Cov(X̄,X₍₁₎)=1/n, not zero. Hence statements 1, 2 and 3 only are true. Other-exam relevance: completeness, minimal sufficiency, ancillary statistics and order statistics are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · complete sufficient statistic in a one-parameter exponential family
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. with density f(x|θ)=(log θ)θˣ/(θ−1), for 0<x<1, where θ>1 is unknown. Let T=∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ. Which description of T is correct?
items.explanation: Write η=log θ, so η>0. The density becomes f(x|η)=ηe^(ηx)/(e^η−1), for 0<x<1. For an independent sample, the joint density is a factor depending on η multiplied by exp(η∑Xᵢ). Thus T=∑Xᵢ is sufficient by factorisation. The natural parameter space η>0 contains an open interval, and this is a full one-parameter exponential family with fixed support. Its natural statistic T is complete as well as sufficient. Therefore option 3 is correct. Other-exam relevance: completeness and sufficiency in one-parameter exponential families are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t7 · Beta-Binomial conjugacy and posterior median
items.stem: Let X have a Binomial(n,p) distribution, where n is known. The prior distribution of p is uniform on [0,1]. Under squared-error loss, the observation is X=n. Which statements are correct?
statements: The Bayes estimate of p is (n+1)/(n+2).
The Bayes estimate of p is 2^(−1/(n+1)).
The median of the posterior distribution of p is 2^(−1/(n+1)).
The median of the posterior distribution of p is (n+1)/(n+2).

A.why: The posterior is Beta(n+1,1), whose mean under squared-error loss is (n+1)/(n+2) and whose median solves p^(n+1)=1/2, giving 2^(−1/(n+1)).

B.why: 2^(−1/(n+1)) is the posterior median, not the posterior mean used under squared-error loss.

C.why: For a Beta(n+1,1) posterior, the CDF is p^(n+1). Setting it equal to 1/2 gives the median 2^(−1/(n+1)).

D.why: (n+1)/(n+2) is the posterior mean, not the posterior median.

items.explanation: A uniform prior is Beta(1,1). Observing X=n means all n trials are successes, so the likelihood is proportional to pⁿ. Multiplying by the prior gives a Beta(n+1,1) posterior. Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean: (n+1)/(n+2), so statement 1 is true. The posterior CDF is F(p)=p^(n+1). The median m satisfies m^(n+1)=1/2, hence m=2^(−1/(n+1)); statement 3 is true. Statements 2 and 4 confuse the posterior mean and median. The correct combination is 1 and 3 only. Other-exam relevance: Beta-Binomial conjugacy and posterior summaries are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t4 · method of moments and constrained Bernoulli maximum likelihood
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables with P(X=x|θ)=θˣ(1−θ)^(1−x), for x=0 or 1 and 0≤θ≤1/2. Which statements are correct?
statements: The method-of-moments estimator of θ is (1/(2n))∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ.
The maximum-likelihood estimator of θ is minᵢXᵢ.
The method-of-moments estimator of θ is minᵢXᵢ.
The maximum-likelihood estimator of θ is min{X̄,1/2}.

A.why: For Bernoulli(θ), E(X)=θ. Equating X̄ to θ gives the method-of-moments estimator X̄, not X̄/2.

B.why: The likelihood depends on the sample through the number of successes, not the minimum observation.

C.why: The minimum of Bernoulli observations is not the method-of-moments estimator.

D.why: Without the parameter restriction, the MLE is X̄. Restricting θ to [0,1/2] projects this value onto the parameter interval, giving min{X̄,1/2}.

items.explanation: For a Bernoulli(θ) variable, E(X)=θ. Equating the sample mean to the theoretical mean gives the method-of-moments estimator θ̂MM=X̄. Therefore statement 1, which has an extra factor 1/2, is false, and statement 3 is false. The likelihood is proportional to θ^(∑Xᵢ)(1−θ)^(n−∑Xᵢ). Its unconstrained maximiser is X̄. Since the allowed parameter space is 0≤θ≤1/2, the constrained maximiser is X̄ if X̄≤1/2 and 1/2 otherwise. This is min{X̄,1/2}, so statement 4 alone is true. Other-exam relevance: method of moments and constrained maximum likelihood are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: inference-t4 · consistency of estimator sequences for a Bernoulli parameter
items.stem: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables with P(Xᵢ=1)=p and P(Xᵢ=0)=1−p, where 0<p<1. Which of the following sequences of estimators are consistent for p as n→∞?
statements: Tₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ.
Tₙ=(Xₙ+Xₙ₊₁)/2.
Tₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ².
Tₙ=(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ(X₂ᵢ₋₁−X₂ᵢ).

A.why: The sample mean of iid Bernoulli(p) variables converges in probability to p by the law of large numbers.

B.why: This average contains only two observations, regardless of how large n becomes. Its variance remains p(1−p)/2, which is positive for 0<p<1, so it does not converge in probability to the constant p.

C.why: A Bernoulli variable takes only 0 and 1, so Xᵢ²=Xᵢ. This sequence is exactly the sample mean in statement 1 and is therefore consistent.

D.why: Each paired difference has expectation E(X₂ᵢ₋₁−X₂ᵢ)=p−p=0. The average of these iid differences converges to 0, not to p, because p>0.

items.explanation:
A sequence of estimators Tₙ is consistent for p if it converges in probability to p as the sample size increases. We examine each sequence.

1. For Tₙ=(1/n)∑Xᵢ, the observations are iid and E(Xᵢ)=p. By the law of large numbers, their sample average converges in probability to E(Xᵢ)=p. Thus statement 1 is true.

2. The estimator (Xₙ+Xₙ₊₁)/2 always uses just two Bernoulli observations. Increasing n changes which two observations are used, but it does not increase the number averaged. Its variance is p(1−p)/2, which does not approach zero for 0<p<1. Therefore it does not concentrate around p and is not consistent. Statement 2 is false.

3. Since a Bernoulli variable can only be 0 or 1, squaring it does not change it: Xᵢ²=Xᵢ. Hence (1/n)∑Xᵢ²=(1/n)∑Xᵢ for every n. This is the same consistent estimator as in statement 1. Statement 3 is true.

4. Let Zᵢ=X₂ᵢ₋₁−X₂ᵢ. The pairs use disjoint independent observations, so the Zᵢ are iid. Also E(Zᵢ)=E(X₂ᵢ₋₁)−E(X₂ᵢ)=p−p=0. By the law of large numbers, their average converges to 0, not to p. Since p>0, statement 4 is false.

Therefore only sequences 1 and 3 are consistent: option A. Other-exam relevance: consistency, Bernoulli sampling and the law of large numbers are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t7 · Bayesian estimation of a normal mean and proper versus improper priors
items.stem: Suppose one observation X follows a normal distribution with unknown mean μ∈ℝ and known variance 1. Under squared-error loss, which statements about the Bayes estimator of μ are correct?
statements: For a proper prior distribution on μ, the resulting Bayes estimator cannot be unbiased for every value of μ.
There exists a proper prior distribution for which the Bayes estimator is unbiased for every value of μ.
Every improper prior distribution necessarily gives a biased Bayes estimator.
There exists an improper prior distribution for which the Bayes estimator is unbiased for every value of μ.

A.why: A proper prior produces a nonconstant marginal density m(x); the posterior mean x + d(log m(x))/dx therefore cannot equal x for every x. The normal location model has X as its unique unbiased estimator, so a proper-prior posterior mean cannot be unbiased for all μ. The flat improper prior gives posterior mean X, which is unbiased.

B.why: No proper prior can give a posterior mean that is unbiased for every μ in this normal location model.

C.why: The flat improper prior π(μ)∝1 gives posterior N(X,1), whose mean is X and is unbiased for μ.

D.why: With the flat improper prior, the likelihood is proportional to exp{−(μ−X)²/2}; normalising it as a posterior gives N(X,1), so the posterior mean is X and Eμ(X)=μ.

items.explanation:
For squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean E(μ|X).

1. Consider first a proper prior π(μ). The marginal density of the observation is m(x)=∫φ(x−μ)π(μ)dμ, where φ is the standard normal density. For this normal location model, the posterior mean can be written as δ(x)=E(μ|X=x)=x + d[log m(x)]/dx. If δ(x) were unbiased for every μ, completeness of the normal location family implies that it must equal the usual unbiased estimator X. That would require d[log m(x)]/dx=0 for all x, so m(x) would have to be constant. A constant function over the whole real line cannot be a proper probability density. Thus a proper prior cannot produce a Bayes estimator that is unbiased for every μ. Statement 1 is true and statement 2 is false.

2. Now use the flat improper prior π(μ)∝1. Multiplying this prior by the likelihood gives π(μ|X=x)∝exp{−(x−μ)²/2}. This is the density kernel of N(x,1). Therefore the posterior mean is δ(x)=x. Since Eμ(X)=μ, this estimator is unbiased. So statement 4 is true and statement 3 is false.

Hence statements 1 and 4 only are correct: option A. Note that 'unbiased' here means unbiased for every μ in the parameter space, not merely having zero bias at one particular parameter value. items.topic: multivariate-t7 · constrained bivariate normal correlation MLE with equal marginal variances
items.stem: Let (X₁,Y₁),…,(Xₙ,Yₙ), n≥4, be a random sample from a bivariate normal distribution with E(Xᵢ)=μ₁, E(Yᵢ)=μ₂, Var(Xᵢ)=Var(Yᵢ)=σ² and Corr(Xᵢ,Yᵢ)=ρ. All four parameters μ₁, μ₂, σ² and ρ are unknown. Define Sₓₓ=∑(Xᵢ−X̄)², Sᵧᵧ=∑(Yᵢ−Ȳ)² and Sₓᵧ=∑(Xᵢ−X̄)(Yᵢ−Ȳ). Which expression is the maximum-likelihood estimator of ρ?
items.explanation:
This model has equal marginal variances, so its covariance matrix is Σ=σ²[[1,ρ],[ρ,1]]. We must estimate the means, the common variance and the correlation together.

Step 1: For a normal sample, the maximum-likelihood estimates of the two means are the sample means X̄ and Ȳ. After centring the observations, define A(ρ)=Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ−2ρSₓᵧ.

Step 2: The determinant of Σ is σ⁴(1−ρ²), and the quadratic part of the log-likelihood is A(ρ)/[σ²(1−ρ²)]. Apart from constants, the log-likelihood is therefore ℓ(σ²,ρ)=−n log(σ²)−(n/2)log(1−ρ²)−A(ρ)/[2σ²(1−ρ²)].

Step 3: For a fixed ρ, differentiate with respect to σ² and set the derivative to zero. This gives σ̂²(ρ)=A(ρ)/[2n(1−ρ²)]. Substitute this expression back into the log-likelihood. The part that depends on ρ becomes −n log A(ρ)+(n/2)log(1−ρ²), up to constants.

Step 4: Differentiate this profile log-likelihood with respect to ρ and set it equal to zero:
2Sₓᵧ/A(ρ)−ρ/(1−ρ²)=0.
Multiplying through gives 2Sₓᵧ(1−ρ²)=ρ[Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ−2ρSₓᵧ]. The terms −2ρ²Sₓᵧ cancel from both sides, leaving 2Sₓᵧ=ρ(Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ).

Therefore ρ̂=2Sₓᵧ/(Sₓₓ+Sᵧᵧ), which is option C. Option A is the usual sample correlation coefficient, but it is not the MLE under the additional equal-marginal-variance restriction in this model. The uncentred expression in option B ignores the unknown means, and option D is not the result of maximising the stated likelihood. items.topic: inference-t4 · consistency of estimators for a Pareto-type model
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be independent and identically distributed with density f(x|θ)=θ/x^(θ+1), x>1, where θ>1 is unknown. Which of the following estimators of θ is consistent?
items.explanation: Take logarithms to simplify the model. If X has density f(x|θ)=θx^(−θ−1), for x>1, then Y=log X has an exponential distribution with rate θ. Hence E(Y)=1/θ. By the law of large numbers, (1/n)∑log(Xᵢ) converges in probability to 1/θ. Since 1/θ is positive, taking the reciprocal gives n/∑log(Xᵢ) → θ in probability. Therefore option D is consistent. The other options do not converge to θ: the first sample mean converges to E(X)=θ/(θ−1), the second to 1/θ, and the third to 1/E(X)=(θ−1)/θ. Source check: the supplied Estimation CSIR NET scan, printed Question 36 on PDF page 16 (26 November 2020), lists these four expressions; the supplied answer-key page lists option 4. items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t4 · factorisation, sufficiency and unbiased estimation for a triangular density
items.stem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ (n≥2) be a random sample from the density fθ(x)=2(θ−x)/θ² for 0≤x≤θ and 0 otherwise, where θ>0 is unknown. Let X̄ be the sample mean and X₍ₙ₎=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which one of the following statements is correct?
items.explanation: The supplied answer list on page 63 gives Question 38 as statement 3. We check the four choices. First calculate the population mean. Evaluating the integral gives E(X)=θ/3: E(X)=∫₀^θ x·2(θ−x)/θ² dx = (2/θ²)[θ·(θ²/2)−(θ³/3)] = θ/3. Therefore E(3X̄)=3E(X̄)=3E(X)=θ, so 3X̄ is unbiased; statement 3 is correct. The maximum X₍ₙ₎ alone is not sufficient: the likelihood contains the factor ∏(θ−Xᵢ), which depends on the individual observations and cannot in general be reduced to the maximum alone. Also, the sample maximum is not unbiased for θ; it is strictly below θ with positive probability and its expectation is below θ. Finally, 3X̄ is not sufficient either, because the likelihood depends on the full product ∏(θ−Xᵢ), not only on the sample sum. Thus option C is the only correct statement. Other-exam relevance: factorisation, sufficient statistics and unbiased estimators are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t1 · inference-t2 · inference-t4 · joint sufficiency, completeness and MLE in a uniform scale family
items.stem: Suppose X₁,…,Xₙ are i.i.d. Uniform(θ,2θ), θ>0. Let X₍₁₎=min(X₁,…,Xₙ) and X₍ₙ₎=max(X₁,…,Xₙ). Which statements are correct?
statements: (X₍₁₎,X₍ₙ₎) is jointly sufficient and complete for θ.
(X₍₁₎,X₍ₙ₎) is jointly sufficient but not complete for θ.
X₍ₙ₎/2 is a maximum-likelihood estimator of θ.
X₍₁₎ is a maximum-likelihood estimator of θ.

A.why: The pair of order statistics is sufficient, but it is not complete.

B.why: The likelihood depends on the sample through the minimum and maximum, so the pair is sufficient. The scale-free ratio X₍ₙ₎/X₍₁₎ is a non-degenerate ancillary function of this pair, which rules out completeness.

C.why: The likelihood is proportional to θ⁻ⁿ on the allowed interval X₍ₙ₎/2≤θ≤X₍₁₎. It decreases as θ increases, so its maximum is at θ=X₍ₙ₎/2.

D.why: The maximum-likelihood estimate is the lower endpoint X₍ₙ₎/2, not X₍₁₎.

items.explanation: The answer list on page 63 gives Question 39 as statements 2 and 3. Step 1: For a Uniform(θ,2θ) observation, the density is 1/θ when θ<x<2θ and zero otherwise. The joint likelihood is therefore L(θ)=θ⁻ⁿ provided every observation lies between θ and 2θ. In terms of the order statistics, this condition is X₍ₙ₎/2≤θ≤X₍₁₎. The likelihood depends on the sample only through the minimum and maximum, so the factorisation theorem shows that (X₍₁₎,X₍ₙ₎) is jointly sufficient. Step 2: It is not complete. The ratio R=X₍ₙ₎/X₍₁₎ has a distribution that does not depend on θ, because multiplying all observations by the scale θ leaves this ratio unchanged. R is non-degenerate. Hence R−E(R) is a non-zero function of the sufficient pair whose expectation is zero for every θ, contradicting completeness. Step 3: Within the allowed interval, L(θ)=θ⁻ⁿ decreases as θ increases. The largest likelihood is therefore attained at the smallest allowed value, θ̂=X₍ₙ₎/2. Statement 3 is true and statement 4 is false. Thus statements 2 and 3 are correct, option B. items.topic: inference-t4 · consistency of variance estimators and the law of large numbers
items.stem: Let X₁,X₂,… be i.i.d. random variables with E(Xᵢ)=0 and Var(Xᵢ)=σ²>0. Which of the following estimators are consistent for σ²?
statements: (1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ(X₂ᵢ₋₁−X₂ᵢ)²
(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ(Xᵢ−X̄)²
(1/n)∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ²

A.why: The squared difference of two independent observations has expectation 2σ², so its average converges to 2σ² rather than σ².

B.why: The centred second moment converges to σ² because the sample mean converges to zero and the average of Xᵢ² converges to E(X²)=σ².

C.why: Since E(X²)=Var(X)+[E(X)]²=σ², the law of large numbers gives (1/n)∑Xᵢ²→σ².

D.why: This is n/(n−1) times the estimator in statement 2, and n/(n−1) tends to one; it has the same probability limit σ².

items.explanation: The supplied answer list on page 63 gives Question 40 as statements 2, 3 and 4. We test each statement using the law of large numbers. Statement 1 uses pairs of independent observations. For each pair, E[(X₂ᵢ₋₁−X₂ᵢ)²]=E(X₂ᵢ₋₁²)+E(X₂ᵢ²)−2E(X₂ᵢ₋₁)E(X₂ᵢ)=σ²+σ²=2σ². Therefore the average of these squared differences converges to 2σ², not σ²; statement 1 is false. For statement 3, E(Xᵢ²)=Var(Xᵢ)+[E(Xᵢ)]²=σ². The law of large numbers gives (1/n)∑Xᵢ²→σ², so statement 3 is true. For statement 2, write (1/n)∑(Xᵢ−X̄)²=(1/n)∑Xᵢ²−X̄². The first term converges to σ² and X̄ converges to E(X)=0, so X̄² converges to zero. Hence statement 2 is true. Statement 4 is n/(n−1) times statement 2. Since n/(n−1)→1, it has the same limit σ² and is also consistent. Thus statements 2, 3 and 4 are correct, option B. items.topic: inference-t7 · Bayesian estimation under squared-error and absolute-error loss with a truncated scale prior
items.stem: Suppose the conditional density of X given θ is f(x|θ)=2x/θ² for 0<x<θ and zero otherwise. The prior distribution of θ is Uniform(0,1). Based on one observation x, which statements about the Bayes estimates are correct?
statements: Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimate is −x logₑx.
Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimate is −x logₑx/(1−x).
Under absolute-error loss, the Bayes estimate is x.
Under absolute-error loss, the Bayes estimate is 2x/(1+x).

A.why: The posterior mean contains the normalising factor 1/(1−x), which is missing from statement 1.

B.why: Squared-error loss is minimised by the posterior mean, and absolute-error loss is minimised by the posterior median. These are −x log(x)/(1−x) and 2x/(1+x), respectively.

C.why: The posterior median is 2x/(1+x), not x.

D.why: The posterior median is found by setting the posterior CDF equal to one-half, which gives 2x/(1+x).

items.explanation: The supplied answer list on page 63 gives Question 41 as statements 2 and 4. First find the posterior distribution. The prior density is constant on 0<θ<1, and the likelihood is proportional to θ⁻² when θ>x. Therefore the posterior density is proportional to θ⁻² on x<θ<1. Its normalising integral is ∫ₓ¹θ⁻²dθ=1/x−1=(1−x)/x. Hence π(θ|x)=x/[(1−x)θ²], for x<θ<1. Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimate is the posterior mean: E(θ|x)=∫ₓ¹θ·x/[(1−x)θ²]dθ = [x/(1−x)]∫ₓ¹(1/θ)dθ = −x log(x)/(1−x). Thus statement 2 is true and statement 1 is false. Under absolute-error loss, any posterior median is a Bayes estimate. The posterior CDF is F(m|x)=[x/(1−x)]∫ₓᵐθ⁻²dθ=(m−x)/[m(1−x)]. Set this equal to 1/2: 2(m−x)=m(1−x), so m(1+x)=2x and m=2x/(1+x). Thus statement 4 is true and statement 3 is false. Therefore statements 2 and 4 are correct, option B. items.topic: design-t1 · one-way random-effects ANOVA; unbiased variance-component estimators versus constrained maximum likelihood
items.stem: Consider the one-way random-effects model Yᵢⱼ=μ+bᵢ+εᵢⱼ, i=1,…,5; j=1,…,10, where bᵢ are i.i.d. N(0,τ²) and εᵢⱼ are i.i.d. N(0,σ²), with all random variables mutually independent. The parameter space is μ∈R, σ²≥0 and τ²≥0. Let σ̂²ᵤ and τ̂²ᵤ be the usual unbiased ANOVA estimators of σ² and τ², and let σ̂²ₘ and τ̂²ₘ be the maximum-likelihood estimators. Which event can occur with positive probability for some parameter values?
statements: σ̂²ᵤ is negative.
τ̂²ᵤ is negative.
σ̂²ₘ is negative.
τ̂²ₘ is negative.

A.why: The unbiased ANOVA estimator of the within-group variance is the within-group mean square, which is a sum of squares divided by positive degrees of freedom and therefore cannot be negative.

B.why: The unbiased estimator of the random-effect variance is (MS_B−MS_W)/10. The between-group mean square can be smaller than the within-group mean square, so this difference can be negative with positive probability.

C.why: The parameter space requires σ²≥0. A maximum-likelihood estimate constrained to this parameter space cannot be negative.

D.why: The parameter space requires τ²≥0. A maximum-likelihood estimate constrained to this parameter space cannot be negative.

items.explanation: The source question is printed as Question 42 (December 2019) on page 19 of the supplied Estimation PDF. The answer list on page 63 gives statement 2 only. To see why, use the balanced one-way random-effects ANOVA formulas. There are a=5 groups and r=10 observations per group. Let MS_W be the within-group mean square and MS_B the between-group mean square. Their expectations are E(MS_W)=σ² and E(MS_B)=σ²+10τ². Therefore the usual unbiased ANOVA estimators are σ̂²ᵤ=MS_W and τ̂²ᵤ=(MS_B−MS_W)/10. The first is a nonnegative sum of squared within-group deviations divided by its degrees of freedom, so it cannot be negative. The second is a difference of two random mean squares. There is positive probability that MS_B<MS_W (for example, when τ²=0), making τ̂²ᵤ negative. This does not imply that the true variance τ² is negative; it reflects that an unbiased estimator is not constrained to be nonnegative in every sample. Finally, the parameter space explicitly requires σ²≥0 and τ²≥0. The maximum-likelihood estimators are maximised over this constrained parameter space, so neither MLE can be negative. Hence statement 2 alone is correct, option B. items.topic: inference-t4 · unbiased estimation of functions of a normal mean and variance
items.stem: Let X₁, X₂ and X₃ be i.i.d. Normal random variables with mean θ and variance θ², where θ∈R is unknown. Which of the following estimators are unbiased for the stated targets?
statements: (X₁+2X₂+3X₃)/6 is unbiased for θ.
(X₁²+4X₂²+9X₃²)/14 is unbiased for θ².
(2X₁+X₃²)/2 is unbiased for θ(1+θ).
X₂(1−X₂/2) is unbiased for θ(1−θ).

A.why: E[(X₁+2X₂+3X₃)/6]=(1+2+3)θ/6=θ, so statement 1 is unbiased.

B.why: E[(X₁²+4X₂²+9X₃²)/14]=(1+4+9)·2θ²/14=2θ², not θ².

C.why: E[(2X₁+X₃²)/2]=(2θ+2θ²)/2=θ(1+θ), so statement 3 is unbiased.

D.why: E[X₂(1−X₂/2)]=θ−(2θ²)/2=θ(1−θ), so statement 4 is unbiased.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 43 (December 2019) on page 20. The answer list on page 63 gives statements 1, 3 and 4. Since E(Xᵢ)=θ and Var(Xᵢ)=θ², we have E(Xᵢ²)=2θ². Statement 1: E[(X₁+2X₂+3X₃)/6]=(1+2+3)θ/6=θ, so it is unbiased. Statement 2: E[(X₁²+4X₂²+9X₃²)/14]=(1+4+9)·2θ²/14=2θ², not θ², so it is biased. Statement 3: E[(2X₁+X₃²)/2]=(2θ+2θ²)/2=θ(1+θ), so it is unbiased. Statement 4: E[X₂(1−X₂/2)]=E(X₂)−E(X₂²)/2=θ−θ²=θ(1−θ), so it is unbiased. Therefore statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct, option B. items.topic: inference-t4 · maximum likelihood with parameter-dependent support and boundary maximisation
items.stem: A random sample of size 7 is drawn from the density fθ(x)=(1+x²)/[3θ(1+θ²)] for −2θ≤x≤θ, θ>0, and zero otherwise. The observations are 12, −54, 26, −2, 24, 17 and −39. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ?
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 44 (June 2019) on page 20, and the supplied answer list on page 63 gives D. First use the support restriction. Every observation must satisfy −2θ≤xᵢ≤θ. The largest positive observation is 26, so θ≥26. The most negative observation is −54, so −54≥−2θ, which gives θ≥27. The other observations impose weaker lower bounds. Thus the full sample is possible only when θ≥27. For a sample of size 7, the likelihood is proportional to [3θ(1+θ²)]⁻⁷ times the product of (1+xᵢ²), provided θ≥27; the product involving the observations is constant with respect to θ. Since θ(1+θ²) is strictly increasing for θ>0, the likelihood decreases as θ increases over the allowed set. It is maximised at the smallest admissible value, θ̂=27. Therefore option D is correct. Other-exam relevance: maximum likelihood, parameter-dependent support and boundary estimates are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. items.topic: inference-t4 · consistency and mean squared error minimisation for a scaled chi-square statistic
items.stem: Let X₁, X₂, … be i.i.d. N(0,σ²), where σ²>0 is unknown. Consider Tₙ=Cₙ∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿXᵢ², with Cₙ>0. Which of the following statements are correct?
statements: Tₙ is consistent for σ² if Cₙ=1/(n−1).
Tₙ is unbiased for σ² if Cₙ=1/n.
Tₙ is consistent for σ² if Cₙ=1/(n+1).
The mean squared error of Tₙ is minimised if Cₙ=1/(n+2).
items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 45 (June 2019) on page 21. The supplied answer list on page 63 ends at Question 44, so no printed answer-key entry for Q45 is available; the answer below is derived directly from the model. Let Sₙ=∑Xᵢ². Since E(Xᵢ²)=σ² and Var(Xᵢ²)=2σ⁴ for a zero-mean normal variable, E(Sₙ)=nσ² and Var(Sₙ)=2nσ⁴. Thus E(Tₙ)=nCₙσ². For Cₙ=1/(n−1), the expectation multiplier n/(n−1) tends to 1; for Cₙ=1/(n+1), n/(n+1) also tends to 1. In both cases, the law of large numbers gives consistency because (1/n)Sₙ→σ² and the extra multiplier tends to 1. For Cₙ=1/n, E(Tₙ)=σ² exactly, so statement 2 is unbiased. Finally, MSE(Tₙ)=Var(Tₙ)+Bias(Tₙ)²=[2nCₙ²+(nCₙ−1)²]σ⁴=[(n²+2n)Cₙ²−2nCₙ+1]σ⁴. Differentiating this quadratic with respect to Cₙ gives the minimiser Cₙ=1/(n+2), so statement 4 is also correct. All four statements are true, option A. items.topic: probability-t8 · inference-t4 · support of a bivariate uniform distribution, dependence versus zero correlation, boundary MLE
items.stem: Let Sθ be the square (diamond-shaped) region with vertices (θ,0), (0,θ), (−θ,0) and (0,−θ), where θ>0 is unknown. Suppose (X,Y) has a uniform distribution on Sθ. Which statements are true?
statements: X and Y are uncorrelated.
X and Y are independent.
|X|+|Y| cannot exceed θ.
For two independent observations (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂), the maximum-likelihood estimate of θ is max{|x₁|+|y₁|, |x₂|+|y₂|}.

A.why: The region and uniform density are symmetric about both axes, so E(X)=E(Y)=0 and E(XY)=0. Hence Cov(X,Y)=0.

B.why: The joint support is the diamond |x|+|y|≤θ, not a Cartesian product of separate X and Y ranges. The variables are dependent even though their covariance is zero.

C.why: This inequality is exactly the support condition defining the diamond-shaped region.

D.why: For two observations the likelihood is proportional to θ⁻⁴ when θ is at least the largest observed L1 distance, and zero otherwise. It decreases with θ, so its maximum is at that smallest admissible value.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 46 (June 2019) on page 22. The supplied answer list on page 63 ends at Question 44, so no printed answer-key entry for Q46 is available; the answer is derived directly from the stated model. The diamond-shaped support is Sθ={(x,y): |x|+|y|≤θ}. By symmetry, E(X)=E(Y)=0 and E(XY)=0. Therefore Cov(X,Y)=E(XY)−E(X)E(Y)=0, so statement A is true. However, zero covariance does not imply independence. Here, if |X| is close to θ, the support forces |Y| to be close to zero; the joint support is not a rectangle of the form A×B, so X and Y are dependent. Statement B is false. Statement C is the support condition itself, so it is true. The area of the diamond is 2θ², hence the density is 1/(2θ²) on the support. For two independent observations, the likelihood is (2θ²)⁻² when θ is at least both observed values of |xᵢ|+|yᵢ|, and zero otherwise. On the allowed range the likelihood decreases as θ increases. Thus the MLE is the smallest admissible θ: max{|x₁|+|y₁|, |x₂|+|y₂|}. Statement D is true. Therefore A, C and D are correct, option C. items.topic: design-t1 · random-intercept model; bias and consistency when the number of clusters is fixed
items.stem: Let b₁,…,b₁₀ be i.i.d. N(0,τ²), and let εᵢⱼ be i.i.d. N(0,σ²), independent of the bᵢ. Define Xᵢⱼ=bᵢ+εᵢⱼ for i=1,…,10 and j=1,…,n. Consider Tₙ=(1/(10n))∑ᵢ₌₁¹⁰∑ⱼ₌₁ⁿXᵢⱼ² as an estimator of σ². Which statements are correct?
statements: Tₙ is unbiased for σ².
Tₙ is consistent for σ² as n→∞.
Tₙ is unbiased for σ² only when τ²=0.
Tₙ is consistent for σ² as n→∞ only when τ²=0.

A.why: E(Xᵢⱼ²)=σ²+τ², so E(Tₙ)=σ²+τ², not σ² when τ²>0.

B.why: With only ten clusters, increasing n estimates each realised bᵢ² contribution more accurately; the average of those ten random effects does not disappear.

C.why: The bias is τ², so the estimator is unbiased exactly when τ²=0.

D.why: As n grows, Tₙ converges to σ²+(1/10)∑bᵢ². This equals σ² almost surely only when τ²=0.

items.explanation: The source prints this as Question 47 (June 2019) on page 23. The supplied answer list on page 63 ends at Question 44, so no printed key is available; the truth values are derived from the model. For each observation, Xᵢⱼ=bᵢ+εᵢⱼ, with independent zero-mean components. Thus E(Xᵢⱼ²)=Var(Xᵢⱼ)=τ²+σ², and E(Tₙ)=τ²+σ². Therefore Tₙ is biased for σ² whenever τ²>0, and it is unbiased only when τ²=0. This makes statement C true and A false. Now keep the number of clusters fixed at 10 and let n increase. Within each cluster, (1/n)∑ⱼXᵢⱼ² converges almost surely to bᵢ²+σ². Averaging over the ten clusters gives Tₙ→σ²+(1/10)∑ᵢ₌₁¹⁰bᵢ² almost surely. If τ²>0, this random-effect contribution does not vanish as n→∞, so Tₙ is not consistent for σ². If τ²=0, all bᵢ are zero almost surely and the limit is σ². Hence statement D is true and B is false. The correct combination is C and D, option C.
